Yes, the story has an appropriate balance between scene and summary/exposition. 

The narrative unfolds primarily as a single, continuous real-time scene—a ferry crossing on the Elbe—complete with vivid sensory details, physical actions, and sparse, realistic dialogue between Ilse and her son, Jonas. Within the natural pauses of this scene, the writer seamlessly weaves brief moments of exposition and summary (such as memories of Jonas as a child, the detail that he now lives in Munich, his habit of arriving unannounced, and the brief mention of Henning's forty-year routine). Instead of halting the momentum with heavy blocks of backstory, the exposition is used just enough to give emotional weight and context to the characters' present-tense interactions.
